clue.text: Yeoman jester's means of raising tip

parts.note: a jack is a device for lifting a car or other heavy load
a point is a sharp tip

explanation.surface: A court fool's way of hoisting the end of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Point is the jester in Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera The Yeomen of the Guard, set at the Tower of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack Point is the name of the professional fool in the Gilbert and Sullivan opera about Tower warders.

clue.text: A longing to hear Schubert's third

parts.note: an itch is a restless craving or longing

explanation.surface: Someone yearns to listen to the third movement of a Schubert work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Schubert's third' is not a symphony but the third letter of the composer's name, H, and the answer is how that letter's name is spelt out; 'to hear' points to the letter as spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: The third letter of the name Schubert is H, and this is the spelling of that letter's name.

clue.text: Sport in which top of kimono receives a tear perhaps

indicators.note: the top of a vertical word is its first letter, so kimono supplies only its opening letter

parts.note: to go at a tear is to go at a great rate, so tear stands for speed or rate

explanation.surface: In a martial art, the jacket of a kimono gets ripped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tear' reads as a rip in the cloth, but here it means a burst of speed, a RATE; 'receives' simply joins K to A RATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Karate is a Japanese martial art practised competitively as a sport.

clue.text: Circles as alternative to scraps

parts.note: the word or introduces an alternative
bits are scraps or small pieces

explanation.surface: Round shapes offered as a substitute for leftovers.
explanation.definitionFit: A planet orbits the sun, travelling round it, so the verb means circles.

clue.text: Perfect numbers?

parts.note: dressed to the ... means dressed perfectly, and the figure in that phrase is a number used in plural

explanation.surface: A question about mathematically perfect numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: In mathematics a perfect number is one like 6 or 28; here 'perfect' points to the idiom 'to the nines', meaning to perfection.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom to the nines means to perfection, and the word is the plural of a number.

clue.text: Build up fire in grate or it will be freezing

indicators.note: to build up a fire is to rearrange the fuel, so the letters of the words are rebuilt into new order

explanation.surface: Stoke up the fire in the grate, or the room will be icy cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Build up' rearranges FIRE IN GRATE OR; 'it will be' is a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Refrigeration is the process of chilling or freezing food to preserve it.

clue.text: Picking up, often at home

parts.note: someone recovering from illness is picking up, and they usually do so resting in their own house

explanation.surface: Collecting something, usually from the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picking up' suggests collecting a parcel; in the cryptic reading it means recovering health, which is mostly done at home.
explanation.definitionFit: Recovering strength gradually after illness is the period of recuperation, frequently spent resting at home.

clue.text: Has no bother in repairing contraption so absurd

indicators.note: repairing means putting something back together, so the letters of these words are reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone has no trouble fixing a ridiculous gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repairing' rearranges HAS NO BOTHER IN into the name of the cartoonist.
explanation.definitionFit: W Heath Robinson drew absurdly elaborate machines, so his name describes any ridiculously complicated contraption.

clue.text: Incite Victor to get a whisk

parts.note: to egg someone on is to incite them
a victor is one who beats an opponent, a beater

explanation.surface: Urge a winner to fetch a kitchen tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victor' looks like the NATO-alphabet V, but it is a winner, one who beats.
explanation.definitionFit: A whisk is a kitchen utensil for whipping eggs or cream, also called by this compound name.

clue.text: Cranks might do this at Wedgwood factory

definitions.text: might do this at Wedgwood factory

explanation.surface: Eccentrics might cause damage at a famous pottery works.
explanation.walkthrough: Wedgwood is a famous English pottery firm; clumsiness there might crack pots.
explanation.definitionFit: Cranks are eccentric people; and in a pottery a careless worker might break the ware.

clue.text: Band that is a cinch in America

explanation.surface: A strap that is easy work in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a cinch' looks like 'an easy task', but in American usage a cinch is also the strap round a horse's belly.
explanation.definitionFit: The strap holding a saddle round a horse's belly is a band, called a cinch in American English.

clue.text: Cut always provided on Sunday

indicators.note: in this across clue on means placed after, so the word for always comes after the day letter

parts.note: ever means always, as in ever hopeful

explanation.surface: A cut that is always granted on the Sabbath.
explanation.definitionFit: To sever something is to cut it through or off.

clue.text: Fail to pay gambling debts? The language!

explanation.surface: Exasperation at a gambler defaulting and at the bad language used.
explanation.walkthrough: To welsh on a bet is to fail to pay it.
explanation.definitionFit: Welching or welshing means dodging a betting debt; and Welsh is the Celtic tongue of Wales.

clue.text: Get by toil and relax, say

indicators.note: say tells the solver the word for relax is to be heard, its spelling changed

explanation.surface: Working hard and then putting your feet up.
explanation.definitionFit: To wrest a living is to extract it with great effort and labour.

clue.text: Ray underweight

explanation.surface: A man named Ray is too thin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ray' looks like a man's name, but it is a beam of light.
explanation.definitionFit: A ray is a beam of illumination; and something underweight weighs little.

clue.text: Door-joint that gives half a turn?

definitions.text: Door-joint that gives half a turn?

parts.words: Door-joint that gives half a turn?
parts.note: the pivot fitting on which a door swings lets it rotate through up to half a full circle

explanation.surface: A door fitting that lets it partly swing round.
explanation.definitionFit: The pivoting joint fixing a door to its frame lets it swing open and shut.

clue.text: Mendicant who has no choice, proverbially

explanation.surface: A pauper with no options, as the saying goes.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'beggars can't be choosers'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mendicant lives by asking for alms; and the proverb says such a person cannot choose.

clue.text: Leaning type-of Pisa, perhaps!

explanation.surface: The Leaning Tower of Pisa, perhaps, set in sloping print.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays on the Leaning Tower of Pisa: sloping print is a leaning typeface, and Pisa is in Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Italic print slopes to the right; and Pisa is an Italian city, so it is of Italy.

clue.text: Marbles champion of Scotland

parts.note: the Scottish earl who removed the Parthenon sculptures to Britain gave his title to them

explanation.surface: The best marbles player in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marbles' suggests the children's game; it means the Parthenon sculptures in the British Museum, named after the Scottish earl who took them. Elgin is also a town in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Parthenon sculptures in London bear the title of the Scottish lord who championed and shipped them.

clue.text: A block to the other side

parts.note: to cross a plan is to thwart or block it

explanation.surface: A barrier placed on the far side.
explanation.definitionFit: Going over a road means passing from one side to the other.

clue.text: Auden's international idle talk

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Auden's international idle talk' for GOSSIP: idle talk defines it, but no parse of 'Auden's international' gives GOSSIP; likely OCR garble, not found online.

clue.text: Tenth article contains it

indicators.note: contains means one word holds another inside it

explanation.surface: A piece of writing that includes the word it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tithe was a levy of one tenth of produce paid to the church.

clue.text: Get on in dire struggle, smoothed over

indicators.note: in places the short word inside the scrambled letters
struggle suggests writhing about, so the letters of dire are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: Getting along in a desperate fight, things were patched up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get' is a link, and 'struggle' makes IRED, the rearrangement of the letters of 'dire', before 'in' places the short word inside. 'smoothed over' means pressed flat.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes pressed with a hot iron are smoothed flat.

clue.text: Cash or credit?

explanation.surface: A shop asks how you would like to pay.
explanation.walkthrough: A bank honours a cheque by cashing it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bank pays out on a cheque it accepts; and credit means esteem or distinction.

clue.text: Eg wide one of the crowd

explanation.surface: An example of something broad, one person among many.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a wide is a ball bowled out of the batter's reach, scoring a run counted among the extras; a film extra plays a member of a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket wide is a run not scored off the bat; and a background actor plays a crowd member.

clue.text: Subject of turns in bank legislation

indicators.note: in tells the solver the answer is sitting inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A topic of reversals in banking law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' suggests policy U-turns, but the joint is what you turn, or sprain, when you trip.
explanation.definitionFit: This joint is the one people most often twist, or turn, when they stumble.

clue.text: It happened in the seventies

indicators.note: in signals that the answer lies inside the word that follows

explanation.surface: Something took place during the 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: An occurrence, something that took place, is an incident or happening.

clue.text: Small and mischievous, the Spanish finish in Paris

parts.note: el is the Spanish word for the
fin is the French word for end, as Paris is a pointer to French

explanation.surface: A cheeky little Spaniard finishes up in the French capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Like a sprite or pixie, something of this kind is tiny and impish.

clue.text: Give the bird to rink-production of Lear? Some reserve here!

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Give the bird to rink-production of Lear? Some reserve here!' for BOOKING OFFICE: BOO + KING is clear, but 'rink-production' looks OCR-garbled and no word gives OFFICE; not found online.
annotationWithheld.clue: Give the bird to rink-production of Lear? Some reserve here!

clue.text: Submitting account for first coat of plaster

explanation.surface: Sending in a bill for the initial layer of plaster on a wall.
explanation.walkthrough: To render an account is to submit it; render is also the first coat of plaster or cement on a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Handing over an invoice is presenting it; and a builder's undercoat on a wall is called render.
